newsitem.title: UK: SAfrica's Stals wary on rates,sees little outflow.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Stals wary on rates,sees little outflow.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said on Thursday he would not take the lead on cutting interest rates unless he saw a slowdown in monetary aggregates.
Speaking in an interview on Reuters Financial Television, he also said there had been only a "very small" amount of capital outflows due to a July 1 foreign exchange control relaxation.
He said that the rand was currently "not a candidate for appreciation" but he added that the central bank did not have a predetermined policy of allowing the rand to weaken.
"The Reserve Bank will not take the lead to bring interest rates down unless there will be some slowdown in the rate of increase in the money supply and in bank credit extension," Stals told RFTV.
He said both these aggregates had levelled out in the last few months but there was no confirmation yet that they were moving down to lower levels.
South Africa's key bank rate is 17 percent and was last moved in November 1996, when it was increased from 16 percent.
Preliminary May M3 money supply growth was 15.40 percent, little changed from a month before, while private sector credit growth slowed to 16.57 percent from 17.4 percent in the same period.
"I think the South African economy is in a period of consolidation, a short term cyclical adjustment that is necessary for the balance of payments," Stals said.
He said he disagreed with comments that he was "too pessimistic" about the economy, specifically in regard to inflation, which he said could ultimately fall below five percent.

On July 1, the central bank relaxed controls to allow individual South Africans to invest as much as 200,000 rand off shore, the first time they were able to export capital since the imposition of exchange control regulations in 1961.
Prior to the July 1 move, the Reserve Bank said the change could spark outflows of three to five billion rand and some economists said the amount could exceed that.
But Stals said that in first 10 days since the relaxation, there had been little outflow.

"The experience for the first two weeks was that it is very small. For the first 10 days or so the amount was only 25 million rand," Stals said. "So South Africans are fortunately not rushing in to take money out of the country at this stage."
Looking beyond individuals, he said South Africa was reaching a stage where bank and financial regulators and supervisors would have to take over prudential policy for institutions.
"The exchange control relaxation will continue and will gradually be replaced by normal prudential requirements."
He said the rand had recently been affacted by negative sentiment towards emerging markets, and declines in the price of gold.
"The problems of a few emerging economies recently had some effect on the exchange rate."

But he added, "Since the end of October last year the rand appreciated for a five-six month period up to the end of March. So in the longer term the rand is not really a candidate for appreciating, taking into account our rate of inflation and cost of production and competitiveness in the world."
Asked if the central bank had a predetermined policy of allowing the rand to depreciate, Stals said:

"No, certainly that is not our policy. We still lean against the wind, we intervene in the markets. We've been buying foreign exchange for some time now to prevent the rand from appreciating more, but with the main purpose to provide liquidity to the market, to smooth out fluctuations and to add to the foreign reserves of the Reserve Bank."
Stals said the central bank had "no predetermined policy target for the exchange rate for the rand."
